bp: A talking-head system tries to make a face in video speak, emote, and move as if it belongs to the audio or driving signal behind it. That matters in avatars, video creation, accessibility tools, telepresence, and also in safety discussions around synthetic media. The problem this paper serves is not generating one more face video. It asks how a fast-moving field can know what it has actually learned. From 2021 to 2025, researchers have built many systems, used many datasets, and invented many measures of quality. Without a shared map, a new builder cannot tell whether the field is mainly solving lip motion, facial expression, style transfer, smooth movement over time, or high visual detail. This survey curates over 100 influential works and organizes them into a semantic taxonomy, so the field can see its own structure rather than treating every new method as an isolated invention.
wh: The hard part is that talking-head generation is not one clean task. A generated face can fail in several different ways. The mouth may match the words but the expression may look flat. The face may look sharp in a single frame but jitter across time. The head pose may follow a driving signal while emotion does not match the speech. A dataset may contain rich audio and video but little emotional variety; another may show emotion but not enough speaker diversity. Evaluation is equally tangled. Measuring frame realism, landmark accuracy, audio-visual synchronization, expression naturalness, and temporal coherence are not the same judgment. If every paper chooses a different dataset and a different score, progress becomes hard to compare. The survey's central difficulty is therefore historical and conceptual: it must turn many uneven research choices into a coherent account of what the community has been optimizing for.
naive: A smart beginner might read the newest papers and rank them by the numbers they report. That fails because the numbers may not be measuring the same thing. One score may reward landmark alignment, another may reward lip synchronization, and another may judge perceptual naturalness. The beginner might instead group papers by method names, such as diffusion models or speech-to-motion systems. That also misses the deeper issue, because the same method family can be used for different goals. A third simple plan is to list datasets and metrics chronologically, but a list alone does not explain why the field moved from frame-level realism toward semantic alignment, temporal coherence, and perceptual quality.
ap: The core idea is to treat the research area itself as the object being analyzed. The paper first curates a corpus of more than 100 influential talking-head works. It then derives a semantic taxonomy, meaning a map organized by what each line of work is trying to represent or control rather than by surface labels alone. The abstract names major directions: speech-to-motion representation, style- and emotion-aware animation, and high-fidelity diffusion models. After building that structure, the paper performs a longitudinal analysis of datasets and metrics from 2021 through 2025. In plain terms, it asks: what kinds of evidence have researchers trained on, what qualities have they measured, and how have those choices changed over time? The central move is joining a conceptual taxonomy with measured historical trends, so future systems can choose datasets and evaluation protocols with a clearer reason.
mech: The mechanism begins with the paper collection. Each work contributes information about its research theme, the datasets it uses, and the metrics or evaluation practices it reports. The survey then sorts the works into a taxonomy. That sorting is semantic: papers are grouped by the meaning of their technical target, such as turning speech into facial motion, controlling style or emotion, or using diffusion-style generation to produce high-fidelity video. Once the taxonomy exists, the authors examine the field across time, from 2021 to 2025. For each period, they track which datasets appear and which metrics are used. This converts a scattered literature into counts and trends: dependence on audio-visual and emotion-rich datasets increases; newly proposed metrics rise quickly; and the newer metrics increasingly target expression naturalness, audio-visual synchronization, landmark accuracy, and driving-signal alignment. The output is not a generated video or a single performance score. It is a structured field map plus a historical measurement of evaluation practice. The paper then uses those patterns to give guidance: if a future system claims to improve talking-head generation, the taxonomy helps say which subproblem it addresses, and the longitudinal metric analysis helps say which evaluation protocol would actually test that claim.
math: The mathematics here is mostly classification, counting over time, and measurement design. Classification means deciding which differences between papers matter. A taxonomy is a controlled sorting rule: two papers belong near each other when they solve the same underlying representation or control problem, not merely because they use similar words. Counting over time turns many individual research choices into a trend. If more papers use emotion-rich datasets after earlier years, that is evidence that the community is valuing emotional behavior more explicitly. Measurement design is the deeper mathematical issue. A metric is a rule that compresses a complex judgment into a number. In talking-head generation, that compression can be dangerous. Landmark accuracy counts whether tracked facial points align, but it may miss whether a viewer experiences the expression as natural. Audio-visual synchronization measures whether mouth movement matches speech timing, but it may ignore style. Temporal coherence asks whether neighboring frames fit together, not just whether each frame looks good alone. The tradeoff is comparability versus completeness: a number lets papers be compared, but it always chooses which kind of failure is visible.
dots: This paper connects to the repo's multimodal vision-language family because talking-head generation depends on several evidence channels cooperating: audio, face images, motion, emotion labels or cues, and sometimes driving signals. The family file describes the shared problem as deciding when unlike signals point to the same real thing. Here, the question is whether speech, facial motion, expression, and visual quality are aligned in the generated video. It also connects to the generative-diffusion family, where generation is described as controlled repair or construction rather than mere realism. The abstract's mention of high-fidelity diffusion models fits that shift: generation is being judged by whether it obeys speech, emotion, and motion constraints. Finally, it connects to the sequence concept, because talking heads are temporal objects. A face that looks correct frame by frame can still fail if expression and motion do not evolve coherently over time.
ww: The approach works because it matches the field's actual confusion. The problem is not that researchers have no results; it is that their results are hard to place beside one another. A semantic taxonomy helps by making hidden task boundaries explicit. Once speech-to-motion representation, emotion-aware animation, and high-fidelity generation are separated, a reader can stop comparing unlike claims as if they were the same. The longitudinal dataset and metric analysis adds a second kind of evidence. Instead of merely asserting that priorities changed, the paper tracks the datasets and metrics researchers used from 2021 to 2025. Those choices reveal what the community found important enough to train on and measure. If newer work proposes more metrics for expression naturalness, synchronization, landmark accuracy, and driving-signal alignment, then the field is moving beyond still-image realism toward whether the generated person behaves meaningfully over time. The survey can therefore guide future evaluation because it identifies both the subproblem and the matching measurement target.
po: The payoff is a practical map for a crowded research area. A future talking-head builder can use the taxonomy to locate the kind of system they are building: speech-driven motion, emotion or style control, high-fidelity generation, or another direction identified in the corpus. They can also use the dataset and metric history to choose a fair evaluation protocol instead of copying whatever score is convenient. The abstract claims this is the first longitudinal analysis of datasets and metrics in talking-head generation from 2021 to 2025, so its value is field coordination: clearer benchmarks, better comparisons, and more meaningful claims about progress.
limits: The paper is a survey, so its strength depends on the corpus and coding choices. The abstract says it curates over 100 influential works, but influence is a selection judgment, and omitted papers could change the picture. A semantic taxonomy is useful only if its categories reflect real technical differences rather than the authors' preferred grouping. Dataset and metric trends show what researchers measured, not necessarily what deployed systems need. The abstract does not prove that newer metrics fully capture human perception, fairness, misuse risk, identity preservation, or cross-cultural expression. It gives guidance for future protocols, but it cannot by itself validate any particular talking-head generator.
